parole.testo: From Latin -issa, borrowed from Ancient Greek -ισσα (-issa), from -ῐᾰ (-ĭă), from Proto-Indo-European *-ih₂, from *-is (i-stem suffix) + *-h₂ (neuter plural suffix). In turn borrowed from Ancient Greek -ισσα (-issa).

parole.significato: alphabet (an ordered set of letters used in a language), especially the Latin alphabet.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin alphabētum (“alphabet”), from Ancient Greek ἀλφάβητος (alphábētos), from ἄλφα (álpha, “alpha”) and βήτα (bḗta, “beta”) (the names of the first two letters in the Greek alphabet). Doublet of алфа́ві́т (alfávít). Compare Ukrainian алфабет (alfabet) (1627), алфабетумъ (alfabetum) (1
From Latin analyticus, from Ancient Greek ἀναλυτικός (analutikós). Compare Russian анали́тик (analítik), Polish analityk.
From Latin anatomia, from Ancient Greek ἀνατομή (anatomḗ, “dissection”), from ἀνά (aná, “up”) + τέμνω (témnō, “to cut, incise”). Compare Russian анато́мия (anatómija), Polish anatomia.
Borrowed from Latin angina, derived from Ancient Greek ἀγχόνη (ankhónē, “strangling”).
Borrowed from Latin anīsum.

Borrowed from Latin apathīa, from Ancient Greek ἀπᾰ́θεια (apắtheia), from ἀπαθής (apathḗs, “without feeling”), from ἀ- (a-, “without”) + πάθος (páthos, “pain”). Compare Russian апа́тия (apátija), Belarusian апа́тыя (apátyja), Polish apatia.
Ultimately from Latin architectūra, from Ancient Greek ἀρχιτέκτων (arkhitéktōn). Cognate with Russian архитекту́ра (arxitektúra), Belarusian архітэкту́ра (arxitektúra), Polish architektura.
Borrowed from Latin astronomus, from Ancient Greek ἀστρονόμος (astronómos).

Derived via Western European languages from Latin atrophia, from Ancient Greek ἀτροφία (atrophía, “a wasting away”), from ἄτροφος (átrophos, “ill-fed, un-nourished”). Compare Russian атрофи́я (atrofíja), Belarusian атрафі́я (atrafíja), Polish atrofia.

parole.significato: aura (the distinctive atmosphere or quality associated with someone or something)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin aura (“a breeze, a breath of air, the air”).
From Latin basis, from Ancient Greek βάσις (básis).
From Latin bacterium, from Ancient Greek βακτήριον (baktḗrion). Compare Russian бакте́рия (baktérija), Belarusian бактэ́рыя (baktéryja), Polish bakteria.
From Latin bronchia + New Latin -ītis, from Ancient Greek βρόγχος (brónkhos) + -ῖτις (-îtis). Compare Russian бронхи́т (bronxít), Belarusian бранхі́т (branxít).
Ultimately from Latin harmonia, from Ancient Greek ἁρμονία (harmonía, “joint, union, agreement, concord of sounds”). Compare Russian гармо́ния (garmónija).
Inherited from Old Ruthenian гермафроди́тъ (hermafrodít), further borrowed from Latin Hermaphrodītus, from Ancient Greek Ἑρμαφρόδῑτος (Hermaphródītos).
Borrowed from Latin glossārium, from Ancient Greek γλῶσσα (glôssa, “tongue”).

parole.significato: rubber (pliable material derived from the sap of the rubber tree)
parole.testo: From Latin gummi/cummi, from Ancient Greek κόμμι (kómmi), from Egyptian qmy (“anointing oil”), qmyt (“acanthus resin, gum”).
Borrowed from Latin hippopotamus, from Ancient Greek ἱπποπόταμος (hippopótamos).

From Latin dysenteria, from Ancient Greek δυσεντερία (dusentería), from δυσ- (dus-, “bad”) + ἔντερα (éntera, “bowels”). Compare Russian дизентери́я (dizenteríja), Belarusian дызентэры́я (dyzjenterýja), Polish dyzenteria.

parole.significato: drama (a composition, normally in prose, telling a story and intended to be represented by actors impersonating the cha…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin drāma, from Ancient Greek δρᾶμα (drâma).
Ultimately from Latin dromas, dromadis, from Ancient Greek δρομᾰ́ς, δρομᾰ́δος (dromắs, dromắdos). Doublet of дромеда́р (dromedár).
Derived via Western European languages from Latin diabētēs, from Ancient Greek διαβήτης (diabḗtēs). Compare Russian диабе́т (diabét), Belarusian дыябе́т (dyjabjét).

From діагона́ль (diahonálʹ) + -ний (-nyj), from Latin diagōnālis, from Ancient Greek διαγώνιος (diagṓnios). Compare Russian диагона́льный (diagonálʹnyj), Belarusian дыягана́льны (dyjahanálʹny), Polish diagonalny.

From Latin diametrus, from Ancient Greek διάμετρος γραμμή (diámetros grammḗ, “line measuring across”), from διά (diá, “across”) + μέτρον (métron, “measure”). Compare Russian диа́метр (diámetr), Belarusian дыя́метр (dyjámjetr).
Borrowed from Latin diaeta, from Ancient Greek δῐ́αιτᾰ (dĭ́aită). Compare Russian дие́та (dijéta), Belarusian дые́та (dyjéta), Polish dieta.

Learned borrowing from Latin eczema, from Ancient Greek ἔκζεμᾰ (ékzemă, “cutaneous eruption”), from ἐκζέω (ekzéō, “to boil out, break out”) + -μᾰ (-mă, nominal suffix). Compare Russian экзе́ма (ekzéma), Belarusian экзэ́ма (ekzéma).
Ultimately from Latin oeconomia, from Ancient Greek οἰκονομία (oikonomía, “management of a household, administration”), from οἶκος (oîkos, “house”) and νόμος (nómos, “law”), with -іка (-ika).

Borrowed from Latin oeconomia, from Ancient Greek οἰκονομία (oikonomía, “management of a household, administration”), from οἶκος (oîkos, “house”) and νόμος (nómos, “law”). Compare Russian эконо́мия (ekonómija).
From Latin emblēma, from Ancient Greek ἔμβλημα (émblēma). Compare Russian эмбле́ма (embléma).
Derived via Western European languages from Latin epilogus, from Ancient Greek ἐπίλογος (epílogos). Compare Russian эпило́г (epilóg), Belarusian эпіло́г (epilóh).
Borrowed from Latin ēthica, from Ancient Greek ἠθική (ēthikḗ).

Inherited from Old Ruthenian етѵмоло́ґїа (etimológia), further borrowed Latin etymologia, from Ancient Greek ἐτυμολογία (etumología), from ἔτυμον (étumon, “true sense”) and -λογία (-logía, “study of”), from λόγος (lógos, “word; explanation”). Featuring the -логія (-lohija) ending.

parole.significato: cell (a room in a prison or jail for one or more inmates)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin camera.

parole.significato: cannabis (mildly euphoriant or sedating, intoxicating hallucinogenic drug prepared from Cannabis plants)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin cannabis (“hemp”), from Ancient Greek κάνναβις (kánnabis).
Borrowed from Latin catastropha, from Ancient Greek καταστροφή (katastrophḗ), from καταστρέφω (katastréphō, “to overturn”), from κατά (katá, “down, against”) + στρέφω (stréphō, “to turn”).

Internationalism ultimately from Latin catēgoria, from Ancient Greek κατηγορία (katēgoría). Compare Russian категориза́ция (kategorizácija), Belarusian катэгарыза́цыя (kateharyzácyja), Polish kategoryzacja.
From Latin clitoris, from Ancient Greek κλειτορίς (kleitorís).
Borrowed from Latin colossus, from Ancient Greek κολοσσός (kolossós, “large statue, especially the colossus of Rhodes”)
From Latin comma, from Ancient Greek κόμμα (kómma), from κόπτω (kóptō, “to cut”).
Borrowed from Latin comēta, comētēs, from Ancient Greek κομήτης (komḗtēs).
Borrowed from Latin cōnus, from Ancient Greek κῶνος (kônos).
Derived via Western European languages from Latin crātēr, from Ancient Greek κρᾱτήρ (krātḗr).
Ultimately from Latin critērium, from Ancient Greek κριτήριον (kritḗrion). Compare Russian крите́рий (kritérij), Belarusian крытэ́рый (krytéryj).

parole.significato: leopard (a large wild cat with a spotted coat, Panthera pardus)
parole.testo: Derived via Western European languages from Latin leopardus, from Ancient Greek λεόπαρδος (leópardos).
Borrowed from Latin lōtos, lōtus (possibly via German Lotos), from Ancient Greek λωτός (lōtós).
Internationalism ultimately from Latin lympha and Ancient Greek κύτος (kútos).
Ultimately from Latin lītūrgia, from Ancient Greek λειτουργῐ́ᾱ (leitourgĭ́ā).
From Latin marmor, from Ancient Greek μάρμαρος (mármaros, “marble, crystalline rock”). Compare Russian мра́мор (mrámor), Polish marmur.
Derived via Western European languages from Latin massa, from Ancient Greek μάζα (máza).
Borrowed from Latin amygdalum, from Ancient Greek ἀμύγδαλον (amúgdalon). Compare Polish migdał, Russian минда́ль (mindálʹ), Belarusian мінда́ль (mindálʹ).
Probably borrowed from Latin Mūsa, from Ancient Greek Μοῦσα (Moûsa).
Borrowed from Latin opium.
Learned borrowing from Latin opium.
Derived via Western European languages from Latin orgia, from Ancient Greek ὄργῐᾰ (órgĭă). Compare Russian о́ргия (órgija).
From Latin paedagōgus, from Ancient Greek παιδαγωγός (paidagōgós).

parole.significato: podium (a platform for presenting awards and also a place for speakers to perform in front of a mass audience)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin podium.
Ultimately from Latin poēma, from Ancient Greek ποίημα (poíēma). Compare Russian поэ́ма (poéma).

parole.significato: pole (either of the two points on the earth's surface around which it rotates)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin polus, from Ancient Greek πόλος (pólos).
Derived via Western European languages from Latin prisma, from Ancient Greek πρίσμα (prísma, “something sawed”), from πρίω (príō, “to saw”).

parole.significato: pygmy (a member of various African peoples)
parole.testo: From Latin Pygmaeī, from Ancient Greek πυγμαῖος (pugmaîos, “a member of a race of dwarves”), from πυγμή (pugmḗ, “fist (as small as a fist)”).
From Latin pȳramis, pȳramidis, from Ancient Greek πῡραμίς (pūramís), πῡραμίδος (pūramídos). Compare Russian пирами́да (piramída), Polish piramida.

parole.significato: python (any member of the family Pythonidae of nonvenomous constrictor snakes)
parole.testo: Internationalism from Latin pȳthōn, from Ancient Greek Πύθων (Púthōn, “Python”), from Πυθώ (Puthṓ), ancient name of Delphi.

From Latin rhētorica, from Ancient Greek ῥητορική (rhētorikḗ), ellipsis of ῥητορικὴ τέχνη (rhētorikḕ tékhnē), from ῥητορικός (rhētorikós, “concerning public speech”), from ῥήτωρ (rhḗtōr, “public speaker”).
Borrowed from Latin salamandra, from Ancient Greek σαλαμάνδρα (salamándra), from Persian سمندر (samandar).

parole.significato: satrap, a governor of a province in ancient Persia and Media
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin satrapēs (“governor”), from Ancient Greek σατράπης (satrápēs).
From Latin symphōnia, from Ancient Greek συμφωνία (sumphōnía). Compare Russian симфо́ния (simfónija), Belarusian сімфо́нія (simfónija).

From Latin synōnymum, from Ancient Greek συνώνυμον (sunṓnumon), neuter singular form of συνώνυμος (sunṓnumos, “synonymous”), from σύν (sún, “with”) + ὄνομα (ónoma, “name”). Compare Russian сино́ним (sinónim), Belarusian сіно́нім (sinónim), Polish synonim.
From Latin synthesis, from Ancient Greek σύνθεσις (súnthesis, “putting together; composition”).
From Latin systēma, ultimately from Ancient Greek σύστημα (sústēma). Compare Russian систематиза́ция (sistematizácija), Belarusian сістэматыза́цыя (sistematyzácyja), Polish systematyzacja.
Derived via Western European languages from Latin stōicus, from Ancient Greek Στωϊκός (Stōïkós). Compare Russian сто́ик (stóik), Belarusian сто́ік (stóik), Czech, Polish, and Slovak stoik.
From Latin thalamus, from Ancient Greek θάλαμος (thálamos).
From Latin thesis, from Ancient Greek θέσῐς (thésĭs).
Derived via Western European languages from Latin theōrēticus, from Ancient Greek θεωρητικός (theōrētikós).

parole.significato: slag heap, spoil heap, spoil tip (heap formed of material discarded during mining or excavation)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin terra (“land”) and Ancient Greek κῶνος (kônos, “cone”). Melnychuk claims a borrowing from French terriconique. Compare Russian террико́н (terrikón), Belarusian тэрыко́н (terykón).
Derived via Western European languages (English toxin, French toxine) ultimately from Latin toxicum, from Ancient Greek τοξικός (toxikós).
Borrowed from Latin trigōnometria, from Ancient Greek τρίγωνον (trígōnon, “triangle”) + -metria (“-metry”).

parole.significato: troglodyte (a member of a supposed prehistoric race that lived in caves or holes, a caveman)
parole.testo: Derived via Western European languages from Latin Trōglodytae, from Ancient Greek τρωγλοδύτης (trōglodútēs).
Derived via Western European languages from Latin thronus, from Ancient Greek θρόνος (thrónos, “chair, throne”).
PIE word  *tréyes From Latin tri- (“three”) and Ancient Greek τρι- (tri-, “three”).
Borrowed from Latin phantasia.
From Latin physicus, from Ancient Greek φυσικός (phusikós). Compare Russian фи́зик (fízik), Belarusian фі́зік (fízik), Polish fizyk.
Borrowed from Latin physica, from Ancient Greek φυσική (phusikḗ). Compare Russian фи́зика (fízika), Belarusian фі́зіка (fízika), Polish fizyka.

Borrowed from Latin physiologia, from Ancient Greek φυσιολογία (phusiología), with -ло́гія (-lóhija) ending from Ancient Greek -λογία (-logía). Compare Russian физиоло́гия (fiziológija), Belarusian фізіяло́гія (fizijalóhija), Polish fizjologia.
From Latin cholera (“bilious disease”), from Ancient Greek χολέρα (kholéra, “cholera”).

parole.significato: chrestomathy, reader (collection of written passages compiled as a study guide)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin chrēstomathia, from Ancient Greek χρηστομάθεια (khrēstomátheia). Compare Russian хрестома́тия (xrestomátija), Belarusian хрэстама́тыя (xrestamátyja), Polish chrestomatia.
Borrowed from Latin centrum.
Borrowed from Latin cyclus.
Borrowed from Latin cyclōps, from Ancient Greek Κύκλωψ (Kúklōps).
Ultimately from Latin cynicus, from Ancient Greek κυνικός (kunikós). Compare Russian ци́ник (cínik), Belarusian цы́нік (cýnik), Polish cynik.
From Latin idiōta, from Ancient Greek ἰδιώτης (idiṓtēs). Compare Russian идио́т (idiót), Belarusian ідыёт (idyjót).
Ultimately from Latin hypothēca, from Ancient Greek ὑποθήκη (hupothḗkē). Compare Russian ипоте́ка (ipotéka), Polish hipoteka.
Derived via Western European languages from Latin īrōnīa, from Ancient Greek εἰρωνεία (eirōneía). Compare Russian иро́ния (irónija), Polish ironia.
